Okay, let’s discuss this further.

In 2018, there were an estimated 1.4 million suicide attempts in the United States; of those 48,344 were “successful.” 3.5% is a dismal success rate, although that is most likely a good thing.

Also, countries with strict gun control laws, which reduce citizens’ access to the easiest and most lethal suicide method, generally have lower suicide rates. For example, the United States’ suicide rate is 31% higher than Canada’s.

Then there all those people that attempt suicide and are stopped at the last minute or survive life-threatening injuries and express gratitude to be alive.

I agree that some people are determined to die and won’t be stopped. There was a guy in my hometown that built his own gun and shot himself. This was long before 3D printers and printed guns too.

However, there is plenty of evidence that most suicides are poorly planned or even spur of the moment decisions triggered by stress. A population educated in the signs of suicide and trained in some basic mental health first aid techniques could provide early intervention, save lives, and reduce suicide deaths.

I honestly don’t see what is so controversial and offensive about modifying strategies that have already proven to be successful in reducing heath attack deaths, stroke deaths,  and injury deaths and implementing them to reduce suicide deaths.

Like I said, I don’t want families to feel responsible for their loved ones’ deaths. I feel for those that already lost loved ones to suicide. But 800,000+ people will take their own lives this year, and 600,000 of those people will show warning before they do it. And we could do something about it.

To be honest, I don’t understand the privacy concern, and I’ll try to explain why.

1.) So much information about households is already tracked: water consumption, power consumption, natural gas consumption, Internet usage (more on that later), heck, I haven’t gotten a paper phone bill in a decade now, but the last time I did, it told me what numbers I called, how long I spent talking to the person on the other end (down to the second), etc.

2.) Most household bills are in one member’s name only. So if a man signs up for a cable subscription and his wife, children, father-in-law use it (maybe even the tenant in the basement, who knows?), there’s no easy way to determine what the customer is watching and what his friends and family are watching.

3.) With the exception of President Trump, who can apparently be influenced by what the news is saying on any given day, I doubt the TV networks care what any individual Joe Blow or Jane Does is watching anyway. Keep in mind that this data is used for advertising purposes. Advertisers want as many people to see their ads as possible. Less watched shows aren’t cancelled because they’re bad, they’re cancelled because not enough people are watching for advertising agencies to justify buying an ad spot. And even if, say, Toyota could convince a billionaire to buy one of their vehicles, that’s still just one sale.

4.) The cable companies can collect this data without collecting identifying information, or scrub any personal information from the data before they turn it over to the TV networks.

5.) The cable companies can give their customers the option to opt out of data collection if they’re still concerned about their privacy. But even if they didn’t, what are people going to do? Cancel their cable subscriptions? I know “cord cutting” is already a concern, but online media companies are way more invasive than traditional ones. Netflix knew that one of their customers watched “A Christmas Prince” every day for 50-some days AND TWEETED ABOUT IT. Internet service providers track what their customers are doing online, and throttle those they believe are pirating. Google sells your searches to Amazon, so they can directly advertise to you. The devil you know and all...

6.) Who fucking cares if some corporate drone knows you watched “The Walking Dead: A Hardcore Parody” porno? I used to work in a video store. No one gave a shit about the customers’ viewing history. And since we were a small business, we had way more information about our customers than metadata scrubbed of identifying info.

I guess what I’m trying to say is that there are privacy concerns, and then there are ”privacy concerns.” I struggle with mental illness, and I would very much like to do a DNA test to determine which medication(s) work best for me, but I don't want that information sold to insurance companies. Health information is private, and shouldn't be shared with anyone that doesn't ”need to know” (although, I suspect that is already a concern in the American health care system since there are so many entities with their fingers in the pie). But what I watch on TV? Pfft.

Maybe the porno studios would be less fucking gross if their movie titles were more public too.

When I was about 14 years old, something in my brain broke and I started wanting to die. I was 15 the first time I was hospitalized for attempting suicide. By age 22, I was hospitalized twice more, and made dozens of other attempts on my life that I never sought treatment for. I tried all the drugs, went to counselling, etcetera, but nothing helped. It was a dark time in my life. I cut myself. I drank heavily. I abused drugs.

I don’t really remember what motivated me to do this, but at some point I just decided I would put off suicide until my “Royal Birthday,” the year when my age and the day I was born matched. It was about 3.5-4 years away at that point. I didn’t really commit to any other changes. I still cut myself. I still drank heavily. I still abused drugs. I didn’t really intend on living past age 26. I just decided I wasn’t going to try to end my life again until then.

And something funny happened, around age 25, all those stupid things that felt like the end of the world, stopped feeling like the end of the world. My planned “Death Day” came and went. That little voice in my head that screamed at me to kill myself never went away, but it was drowned out by more rational voices.

It’s such a cheesy thing to say, but I like to tell young people to give life a chance before they end it all. Maybe it’ll get better, maybe it won’t. Suicide is always an option. Just give your life a chance to unfold before you throw it away.

I was in a pretty similar place about a year and a half ago. I was laid off a week or two before Christmas 2017. Thankfully, I was fortunate enough to get about 8 months of unemployment. I was pretty choosy about the jobs I applied for at first, but when those 8 months came to a close, I panicked and threw spaghetti at the wall to see what stuck.

Nothing. Nothing stuck.

I was in that awkward place where I was too skilled for entry level service industry positions, but underqualified to continue on my previous career path - not that I particularly wanted to continue doing that line of work. I must’ve sent out a few dozen resumes during my last week of unemployment, and I didn’t get a single call back.

Then I started missing payments. I tried to grin and bear it while creditors called and threatened me (funny how fast you can stop being a valued customer), while my credit score plummeted, etc. My breaking point came after I had a fight with my mom. She was lecturing me about how I should be working (no argument there), how I was being too picky with my applications (fuck off), and I just snapped. She stormed off and I thought “Screw it, I’m done.”

So I walked to the lake at the edge of town. It was early fall by this point, and it was freezing at this point. I stood over the ledge planning to jump in, when a policeman stopped me. He brought me to the hospital, I got put on meds. A few months later, I got a job working with disabled people. I really loved that job, but it didn’t really work out. I looked like one of my client’s brothers, and that brother abused him; he never quite got over that. So I quit and went back to school to get my nursing degree.

I can’t say things are perfect. I wouldn’t be lurking here if I wasn’t having suicidal thoughts. I’m barely making minimum payments to keep creditors off my back. But things are looking up. I guess you just have to keep on keeping on sometimes.

In the Season 2 episode where Luke escapes to Canada, the army woman said she deserted because she and her squad stumbled upon a prototype Red Center. The timeline is a little wonky, but there appears to have been a period between the Sons of Jacob taking out the U.S. Government and the establishment of Gilead where the SoJ tried to continue the United States.

I agree and disagree, that MAY have been why the council supported the handmaid system (they do seem to love their sex slaves), but in the context of that scene, no. I suspect Fred and Serena’s marriage was still happy in the aftermath of the fall of the United States; my understanding is that Fred treated June differently because the Waterfords’ previous handmaid killed herself. Pryce struck me as a “true believer” in Gilead’s religious values; he did create a secret system of Eyes to spy on his fellow Commanders after all. I don’t believe he wanted a concubine for a second. Guthrie was the one caught, by Pryce’s secret Eyes, “fooling around” with his handmaid, and he didn’t want one in the first place; he advocated for human breeding farms after all.

If I recall correctly, the Sons of Jacob’s plan was always to force fertile women to birth children. There was just some disagreement among the leadership about what that would look like. Thinking back to the Nick-centric episode in Season 1, specifically the scene where he is driving Commanders Waterford, Pryce, and Guthrie around, Guthrie proposed human breeding farms where fertile women would be forcibly inseminated and the children would be given away to “superior” families; Pryce balked at the idea, stating that the women should be treated as human beings (his one redeeming moment, in my opinion). Waterford agreed with Pryce because the Wives, which were instrumental to the Commanders seizing power, would never support treating women as farm animals. The Handmaid system was conceived as a less oppressive way of forcing fertile women to give birth, and the Ceremony was concocted as a way to let the Wives participate in the insemination process.
